final.title: The hidden cost of results you can’t separate
final.body:
When results are confounded, you pay twice: once in the work itself, and again in the time spent guessing what actually changed. For an owner of a small business, that shows up in ordinary workflows like customer intake, invoice routing, or lead handling, where it is hard to tell whether a bad outcome came from the tool, the process, or the person using it.

That is why this matters in the hire-versus-automation decision. If you cannot separate cause from noise, you cannot budget confidently, you cannot tell whether a tool change helped, and you cannot hand the workflow to someone else with much trust. The problem is not AI hype. It is measurement. And messy measurement makes every decision feel a bit more expensive than it should.

Bareni’s diagnostic is built around that boundary. It starts by identifying one recurring workflow, then says plainly whether AI fits. If it does, the next step is to define success and failure before any pilot is approved. Human approval stays in charge, especially where money or other high-risk decisions are involved.

A practical next step: pick one workflow where the outcome feels muddy, then write down what would count as success, what would count as failure, and what you would need to see before you treat it as a real improvement rather than a lucky week. Which workflow is hardest to audit or hand off?
